reason: A is longer, but it defines every term an outsider needs (ahead check, rollout, fail closed, the load-balancer share) and follows every failure path to its end state, including a failed rollback or a failed canary-off; B leaves those as open questions and relies on a less clear "staging still runs this SHA" check.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but it would serve a newcomer better: it defines the stack terms A assumes you know (pod, rollout, load balancer, Prometheus, squash merge) and walks through every step with its trigger, its locks and its failure path; it also covers cases A leaves as open questions, such as when locks are released after a failure, what happens when canary-off fails, and how to check SSM to recover.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the unfamiliar pieces (Kubernetes deployments and contexts, locks, SSM tags), says what triggers each step, and covers every failure path, including what happens when a recovery command itself fails and how runs that overlap cancel each other. B is easier to skim, but it glosses over these points ("rollout undo if rollout started"), so I would have to guess at how the system really behaves.

author: haiku
reason: B explains more for a newcomer. It defines the Kubernetes and CI terms and gives each step its trigger. It also says why each recovery path is chosen (rollout undo before the SSM tags are written, rollback after) and covers what happens when a recovery command itself fails (HOLD) and when several runs overlap. A is shorter but leaves these gaps, and its rule for when a run is superseded is vaguer.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the same mechanism (deploy.sh, SSM tags, canary, locks, superseding) with a trigger for each step and a short rules section, and its diagram shows every branch, so a newcomer can follow it more easily than A's longer step text and more intricate stale-run rules.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains what each deploy.sh mode actually does (migrate, roll, write SSM, rollback to previous_tag), why migrations, rollbacks and stale-run cancellation are safe, and how cleanup works on failure, so an outsider gets the mechanism and not just the sequence, even though A is shorter and easier to scan.

author: haiku
reason: Document A gives a newcomer a complete picture of how the system runs: concrete timer rates, what "idle" means for a worker, how claims, heartbeats and takeover race, plus a broad failure table. Document B leaves claim frequency and cleanup ownership open and covers fewer edge cases, though its separate constraints list is useful.

author: haiku
reason: B describes how the whole system runs: the timers and poll rates, idle workers running one handler at a time, the handler registry, the overlap when a handler outlives its fence, the race between a sweep and a heartbeat, shutdown, bursts and a broad failure table, whereas A is tighter but leaves key mechanics such as claim frequency and handler behaviour open.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed A, because it covers more of the edge cases and states them more exactly: it gives the waiting-to-retry state its own name, defines the attempt-count check that stops a worker that lost its run from writing (and explains it up front), cancels instead of retrying when a reaped run's schedule is off, and has a fuller failure table; B's summary is friendlier, but it is looser on these points.

author: haiku
reason: B is more complete for a newcomer: it defines more of its terms (handler, fence, partial unique index, in progress), spells out who calls the handler, and covers edge cases A leaves vague, such as a pause during crash recovery, keeping runs still in progress out of the purge, and the explicit retry_wait state, while A's fencing is a little muddled between lease_token and status.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains each mechanism more fully and precisely: why the active-run check is safe under the row lock, the per-candidate reaper lock and re-check, worker_id in the fence, the leftover-queued-run race on resume, and the DB-outage self-lost timer. B reads more easily but leaves those points thin or unaddressed.

author: sonnet
reason: A is tighter, but B explains why each mechanism is safe, for example why the active-run check holds under the schedule lock and how the reaper re-checks a run under lock. It also covers edge cases A skips, such as a DB outage, the worker's self-lost timer, handler timeouts and leftover queued runs after a pause, and its table mapping each requirement to what enforces it gives a newcomer the clearest picture of how the system works.

author: sonnet
reason: A follows a schedule's whole life in order, from save to claim to execute to reap to cleanup, and its glossary names the key mechanisms (the fencing check, the lease and now()) before the steps use them, so a newcomer can understand the system in one pass; B covers slightly more edge cases but scatters the rules, such as save-time checks placed after the loop and a separate retry rule.

author: haiku

reason: A's short glossary, request/shadow flow diagram and tight numbered steps give an outsider a clear picture of the system quickly, while B is more thorough but buries the main flow under a 25-term glossary and many edge cases.

reason: Document A explains the system more precisely and more consistently: it gives the latency budget step by step, says what the shadow job carries so both models see the same features, and says how promotion is pooled over all 7 days and enforced by the registry.
